r4ii_parenthetical.result: Order (1) is implemented correctly and robustly in both tools for every case the ruling specified: a true parenthetical opening directly after the mention's clause binds its numbers (NOVEL-A/NOVEL-F closed), a parenthetical elsewhere in the sentence does not bind, cross-field leakage does not occur, and nested parentheses do not create an evasion. One adjacent robustness gap was found and is NOT a failure of order (1) as specified: any C:V-shaped substring inside a directly-following parenthetical is read as a verse claim even when it is plainly a different kind of reference (a ledger/row id). See T4-01.

vectors_run: t4_true_site_long_distance: a ~200-character single continuous clause naming the real site 41:20 only at the very end -> correctly NOT flagged (no false positive from reading the whole clause)
r4ii_distance_ref.result: citation_sweep's REF arm reads the whole clause (reach=None) exactly as ordered. No true claim was found wrongly RED at any tested distance; a genuinely distant true site number is still recognized correctly.

r4ii_distance_prose_deviation.rule: No code change recommended at this time. A candidate future rule was identified but is UNTESTED by this review and should not be adopted without its own vector construction and adversarial pass: treat an em dash / double-hyphen delimited aside ('-- ... --') the same way a parenthesis is treated for clause-boundary purposes in check_marks' PROSE arm -- i.e. add '--'/'—' to NUM_CLAUSE_END as a hard boundary (which would have correctly excluded P10-008's trailing '41:21' summary clause without any character-count reach), while also extending PAREN_AFTER-style logic to a dash-delimited aside opening directly after the mention's clause (so a genuine disclosure written as 'the puncta extraordinaria -- five dots -- stand at 41:20' is not newly broken). This is a real candidate for closing both directions, but implementing and testing it is out of this review's scope (read-only on the shipped tools) and risks new regressions in dense multi-ref prose that used dashes for other purposes; recorded as a suggested_fix in new_findings, not adopted here.

r4ii_distance_prose_deviation.result: The deviation (PROSE_REACH=60 kept in check_marks, full clause in citation_sweep) is the better trade-off TODAY. It closes a real, already-shipped-adjacent false positive (P10-008-shaped prose is common: a puncta mention followed by an unrelated nearby verse number in the same run-on clause) at the cost of a narrower, already-disclosed false negative (a decoy non-site number more than 60 characters away, on a span that happens to cover the true site, passes silently) that the controlling agent's #e3 ruling already ordered primaries to hand-check. I reproduced both the protected false positive (still silent, correctly) and the residual false negative (still silent, confirming the known gap, empirically) with fresh constructed vectors, not merely by re-reading the ruling's prose. Recommend: accept_deviation, keep the primaries hand-check PERMANENT (matching the orchestrator's own proposed disposition on R4ii-D1) rather than 'until T4 lands', since no adopted-and-tested rule closes both directions yet.

findings: The 'Where Ezekiel's tools differ' paragraph (the one this edit changed) matches the shipped citation_sweep.py and check_marks.py code exactly for every clause I traced: clause-reach split between the two tools, parenthetical-after in both, apposition and parenthesis forms for CAL-1, negation and double-negation handling, and the QERE-tier and MT-qualifier notes. No drift found in the edited paragraph itself.

The book-facts block's sentence 'a claim at those two needs single-witness disclosure' (puncta extraordinaria) is NOT enforced by either tool's PUNCTA arm: unlike the sibling petuchah/setumah, small-letter and paseq arms (which each explicitly check `if "single-witness" not in tail`), citation_sweep.py's and check_marks.py's PUNCTA blocks never test for the phrase. This predates the R4(ii)/CAL-1 edit (the PUNCTA arm's disclosure check was never present, in the adapter's staged code either), was not raised by T1, T2 or T3, and is not live in the current 146-row corpus (all 16 real puncta mentions already carry '(single-witness)' by author discipline, confirmed in the suite-parity run). It is a real documentation/code gap worth closing (add the same single-witness check to the PUNCTA arm, or soften the TOOLKIT.md sentence to 'should carry' until it is machine-enforced), but it is out of R4(ii)/CAL-1's own scope and not a defect this edit introduced.

differences: None against the before-state report's five stated counts (126 / 2 / 3 / 2 / 154) and its 0-puncta / 0-calendar-date claims; every count reproduced exactly on a private copy run with the pinned tools.

One naive keyword hit on 'dateline' inside citation_sweep's problems list is NOT a calendar-date-arm finding: P07-003's problem is a samekh mark-type mismatch whose own quoted ref annotation text happens to contain the word 'dateline' ('hard-seam dateline onset, hayah-perfect word-event form...'). This exact same false hit is independently named in the CAL-1 ruling's own reason field ('the one keyword hit in the 126 is P07-003's samekh claim whose ref text says dateline'), so my independent re-derivation corroborates the controlling agent's prior reading rather than finding something new.

This review confirms aggregate counts only; the before-state report itself was not re-diffed row-by-row against my run's row-level problem/flag lists (both are available in the private report I generated but a full line-by-line diff was not performed, since the brief asks for count confirmation and named differences, and none were found at the count level).

new_findings.artifact: SP\Ezek\tools\citation_sweep.py and SP\Ezek\tools\check_marks.py, PUNCTA arm (puncta_claim_numbers/_range_items via RANGE_NUM)
new_findings.claim: R4(ii) order (1)'s parenthetical-after rule reads ANY C:V/C.V-shaped substring inside the directly-following parenthetical as a verse-number claim, with no check that the parenthetical is actually about puncta at all.
new_findings.evidence: Constructed vector 'the puncta extraordinaria (cross-referenced at row R4.5 in the ledger)' is wrongly flagged in BOTH citation_sweep (ref form) and check_marks (prose form) as 'claims puncta extraordinaria but they stand only at MT 41:20 and MT 46:22 ... the claim names another verse' -- run live against the pinned tools in a private scratch copy, not merely reasoned from the regex.
new_findings.how_verified: Subprocess run of citation_sweep.py and check_marks.py over constructed JSONL rows in my own private scratch (ezek_t4_9f21ab), same invocation pattern _test_zone_tools_ezek.py uses.
new_findings.suggested_fix: Require the parenthetical's number to be paired with a mark-adjacent cue (e.g. only bind when the parenthetical contains nothing but a bare C:V/range and optional 'single-witness', or require a colon-form C:V distinguishable from a dotted id like 'R4.5' by anchoring the chapter to a plausible Ezek chapter 1-48 AND rejecting a leading letter run immediately before the digits). Likelihood in real rows: LOW-MEDIUM -- the campaign's own prose habitually cites ruling/row ids with a similar dotted shape (R4-ii, P10-008, CWO-EZ-10), so a writer referencing such an id inside a parenthetical placed directly after a puncta mention is a plausible, not merely theoretical, authoring pattern.

new_findings.artifact: SP\Ezek\tools\citation_sweep.py puncta_negated() (shared by the PUNCTA arm and, via the same function, the CALENDAR-DATE arm's apposition/parenthesis logic)
new_findings.claim: puncta_negated() only scans for a negation word BEFORE the mention's own position within its clause. A denial phrased with the negating word AFTER the target ('a dateline would be expected but none stands') is not recognized as a negation, so the CAL-1 apposition rule wrongly reads the preceding clause's number as an asserted dateline claim.
new_findings.evidence: Constructed vector 'the unit opens at 45:18, where a dateline would be expected but none stands' is wrongly flagged 'claims a dateline at MT 45:18 - a calendar date with no year word is never a dateline', run live against the pinned citation_sweep.py in a private scratch copy. A control vector targeting an off-list verse ('45:17, and the dateline question is set aside') correctly stays GREEN, isolating the defect to the negation-direction gap rather than to the apposition number-matching itself.
new_findings.how_verified: Subprocess run of citation_sweep.py over constructed JSONL rows in my own private scratch (ezek_t4_9f21ab).
new_findings.suggested_fix: Extend puncta_negated() (or add a forward-looking variant used only by the apposition path) to also recognize a denial word in the clause immediately FOLLOWING the mention when the mention's own preceding clause is what supplies the apposition number -- i.e. when the apposition fallback fires, check both the number's own preceding clause AND the mention's own clause for a negator before accepting the claim as asserted. Likelihood in real rows: MEDIUM-HIGH specifically for MT 45:18, which TOOLKIT.md itself flags as the book's single most actively-discussed near-miss ('Watch MT 45:18 above all ... exactly the combination that reads like an oracle onset'); a primary or author explaining exactly why 45:18 is NOT a dateline is a natural and expected thing to write, and 'X would be expected but none stands' / 'X, though none is present' are ordinary English phrasings for that denial.
